What they do not carry is the paper's larger picture: for finitely many neurons a homeomorphism of the neuron set is only a bijection, "topological simplification" above 1/K is permitted, not shown, and the experiments measure Betti numbers of point clouds at a fixed scale, which the theorem does not protect. The large-step runs show the clouds fragmenting (more components), not merging, and in the Adam runs the step size times the measured top Hessian eigenvalue stays below 0.05 where the topology changes. |
| [LIT-866](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-866.md) | Hyperbolic Entailment Cones for Learning Hierarchical Embeddings | Ganea, Bécigneul and Hofmann (ICML 2018), PMLR 80:1646–1655. Represents a partial order in the Poincaré ball by nested cones: v is below u when v lies in u's cone. Nesting forces apertures of at most π/2 that narrow toward the boundary (r sin ψ/(1 − r²) non-increasing), so cones are undefined near the origin; the widest family is sin ψ = K(1 − r²)/r, with a closed-form membership test. Overlapping cones admit several parents. On WordNet noun closure link prediction in 5–10 dimensions it beats Poincaré and order embeddings once some closure edges are in training; with none, all methods fail. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-671](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-671.md)); worth reading as the paper that represents a partial order, not only a tree, by containment of regions in hyperbolic space. Each concept is a point x of the Poincaré ball and owns a cone S_x, the image under the exponential map of the tangent vectors within an angle ψ(x) of the outward ray through x; v counts as entailed by u when v lies in S_u. Requiring the cones to be axially symmetric, rotation invariant, continuous in aperture and nested (v in S_u implies S_v inside S_u) forces ψ ≤ π/2 (Lemma 2) and makes r sin ψ(r)/(1 − r²) non-increasing (Theorem 3), so no cone can be defined near the origin; the widest family is sin ψ(x) = K(1 − ‖x‖²)/‖x‖ outside a ball of radius ε, and membership is a closed-form angle test (Theorem 5). That family is transitive (Theorem 4), but the proof is only said to be "similar" and is not given. Cones of incomparable points can overlap, so a node may sit below several parents. The evidence that learned cones fit a DAG is one WordNet-noun experiment: held-out edges of the transitive closure, test F1 at 5 and 10 dimensions, single runs, where hyperbolic cones lead once 10% or more of the closure is in training but every method fails (F1 27–43%) when only the transitive reduction is, and Euclidean cones initialised from Poincaré embeddings match the hyperbolic ones. |
| [LIT-867](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-867.md) | Emergent Hyperbolic Network Geometry | Bianconi and Rahmede (2017), Scientific Reports 7, 41974. Growing simplicial complexes, made by gluing d-simplices to (d − 1)-faces with probability ∝ 1 + s n_α (flavor s = −1, 0, 1), have a tree as their dual and, drawn with equal links as ideal simplices in the Poincaré ball, fill hyperbolic d-space: the hyperbolic geometry is an outcome of a purely combinatorial rule rather than its cause. Degrees are exponential for d + s = 1 and power-law with γ = 2 + 1/(d + s − 1) ≤ 3 for d + s > 1; clustering and modularity are high for d ≥ 2. Hyperbolicity is shown by construction, conditional on equal link lengths, not proved. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-678](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-678.md)); worth reading as the model that turns the hidden-metric account of complex networks around: a simplicial complex grown by gluing d-simplices to (d − 1)-faces, with no geometry in the rule, comes out small-world, clustered, modular and (for d + s > 1) scale-free, with γ = 2 + 1/(d + s − 1) from a master equation. Its dual is a tree, so with every link given equal length each simplex is drawn as an ideal simplex of the Poincaré ball and each new node at the normalised sum of its parent face's positions. That embedding, not a proof, is the paper's case that the geometry is hyperbolic, and the authors concede it rests on the equal-length assumption (unequal lengths fit a sphere) and that the ideal-simplex distances are infinite. A fitness on faces gives a numerically observed transition in which the complex grows in one direction. |
| [LIT-870](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-870.md) | Hyperbolic Diffusion Embedding and Distance for Hierarchical Representation Learning | Lin, Coifman, Mishne and Talmon (2023), ICML 2023 (PMLR 202), [ARXIV-2305.18962](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18962). Recovers a latent tree from point-cloud or graph data without learning: diffusion densities at dyadic time scales are embedded in a product of Poincaré half-spaces, and the ℓ1 product distance, a scale-weighted Hellinger sum, is proved equivalent up to constants to a thresholded snowflake min{1, d_T^(2α)} of the tree metric when the operator behaves like the heat kernel on a tree. It keeps local tree neighbourhoods (best MAP on the benchmarks) but not global distances (higher distortion than hyperbolic MDS). | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-675](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-675.md)); worth reading as a construction that recovers a latent tree from unlabelled data by distances alone, with a proof of what is recovered. Each point is represented by its diffusion densities P^(2^−k) e_i at dyadic times, each density is placed in a Poincaré half-space at a height set by its scale, and the hyperbolic diffusion distance is the ℓ1 sum over scales of the hyperbolic distances, 2 sinh⁻¹(2^(1−kα)‖φ_i^k − φ_j^k‖) with φ the square roots of the densities, a scale-weighted Hellinger distance. Theorem 1 (Appendix C, after Leeb and Coifman) says that for the heat kernel on a tree this is equivalent up to constants to min{1, d_T^(2α)}, 0 < α < 1/2: a thresholded snowflake of the tree metric, not the tree metric, and saturated beyond a fixed radius; the main text states it without the threshold. The tree heat-kernel bounds are stated, not proved, and one step of the Hölder bound (Proposition C.5) holds only for tree distances of at least 1, so the admissible range of α is not secured. Empirically it gives the best mean average precision on five graph benchmarks and two single-cell datasets and worse average distortion than hyperbolic MDS or Sarkar's construction: local neighbourhoods are kept, global distances are not. Nothing in it concerns attributes or linear directions. |
| [LIT-872](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-872.md) | Hyperbolic geometry of the olfactory space | Zhou, Smith & Sharpee (2018), Science Advances 4(8):eaaq1458. In four natural odour sources the rank order of correlations between compound concentrations has the clique-topology signature of points near the surface of a 3D hyperbolic ball and not of a uniform Euclidean cube, and human perceptual descriptions of 127 odorants have that of a full 3D hyperbolic ball. Pleasantness, boiling point and acidity read out as linear axes of the fitted fruit-odour space. The hierarchy that motivates the hyperbolic model is argued from biochemistry, not recovered from the data. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-672](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-672.md)); worth reading as the first application of clique topology to stimulus statistics rather than neural data, and as the Sharpee lab's first claim of a hyperbolic geometry in biology. For four natural odour sources (strawberry, tomato, blueberry, mouse urine; 45–78 compounds over 50–101 samples), the rank order of absolute concentration correlations gives Betti curves that match points sampled near the surface of a 3D hyperbolic ball (R_max = 7, R_min = 0.9 R_max, the same for all four) and reject uniform Euclidean cubes of any dimension tried. Human descriptor profiles for 127 odorants (Dravnieks) match a full 3D hyperbolic ball and no Euclidean cube. Linear axes for pleasantness, boiling point and acidity are found in the fitted fruit-odour space. The tree that motivates the hyperbolic model is argued, not recovered: compounds do not cluster by chemical class, and the only null geometry is a uniform Euclidean cube. |
| [LIT-874](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-874.md) | Representation Tradeoffs for Hyperbolic Embeddings | Sala, De Sa, Gu and Ré (ICML 2018), PMLR 80:4460–4469. Trees embed in the hyperbolic plane with distortion 1 + ε (Sarkar's construction), but a hyperbolic distance d costs about d bits, so the embedding needs Θ((ℓ/ε) log deg_max) bits per coordinate in the plane: logarithmic in branching, linear in depth (lower bound proved for H², with an approximation). Higher dimension, via coding-theoretic child placement, divides the upper bound by r. Also an exact hyperbolic MDS by PCA after centring at a new mean, with a perturbation bound growing as sinh²(diameter), and a local-convexity condition for hyperbolic PGA. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-679](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-679.md)); worth reading as a quantitative account of why trees fit hyperbolic space and what the fit costs. Following Sarkar, any finite tree embeds in the hyperbolic plane with worst-case distortion at most 1 + ε by placing each node's children evenly on a hyperbolic circle of radius τ around it; but a hyperbolic distance d needs about d bits to write down, so the coordinates need O((ℓ/ε) log deg_max) bits, ℓ the longest path, and an explicit tree of deg_max chains shows Ω((ℓ/ε) log deg_max) is needed in the plane. Precision grows with the logarithm of the branching and linearly with depth: hyperbolic space is cheap for short bushy hierarchies and dear for long chains. In r dimensions, children placed on hypercube vertices chosen by a Hadamard code divide the cost by r up to r ≈ log deg_max (upper bound only). For general metrics it gives an exact hyperbolic MDS: cosh of the distances is uuᵀ − XXᵀ once the points are centred at a new pseudo-Euclidean mean, so PCA recovers them. The lower bound's proof uses a small-angle approximation and covers only the plane; the PGA guarantee is local convexity, not global recovery; the experiments, including the WordNet MAP of 0.989 in two dimensions, are reported at ε = 0.1, where WordNet takes 2,877 bits per coordinate, while the introduction quotes the ε = 1 figure of about 500. |
| [LIT-875](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-875.md) | An argument for hyperbolic geometry in neural circuits | Sharpee (2019 online), Curr. Opin. Neurobiol. 58:101–104. A four-page review arguing that neural and other biological circuits should have hyperbolic geometry, because hyperbolic space approximates trees, hyperbolic networks are navigable, and Zipf's law, read as states growing exponentially with log-improbability and taken as the mark of maximally informative, latent-driven systems, shares that exponential growth. Its evidence is the olfactory embedding of Zhou, Smith & Sharpee (2018) and earlier perception work; the Zipf-to-hyperbolic link is an analogy, not a derivation. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-670](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-670.md)); worth reading as the short programmatic statement, by the lab behind the olfactory and hippocampal hyperbolic findings, of why hyperbolic geometry should be expected in neural circuits, and as a map of the literatures it joins: hyperbolic random graphs and greedy routing, Zipf's law and statistical criticality, and maximally informative representations. Its own argument is a chain of analogies, not a derivation. Zipf's law is rewritten as a count of states growing exponentially with energy (−log probability), and exponential growth of states is a hallmark of trees and of hyperbolic space, so the two are said to be connected; but exponential growth of states holds for any system with extensive entropy, and what singles out Zipf (unit slope) plays no part in the step to geometry. A rigidity argument for three dimensions cites Mostow's theorem, which concerns finite-volume hyperbolic manifolds of every dimension ≥ 3 and says nothing about point clouds. The one piece of data, a 3D Poincaré-ball embedding of fruit odorants with a pleasantness gradient, is reproduced from Zhou, Smith & Sharpee (2018). |
| [LIT-876](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-876.md) | Hippocampal spatial representations exhibit a hyperbolic geometry that expands with experience | Zhang, Rich, Lee & Sharpee (2022 online, Nat. Neurosci. 26, 2023). The pairwise correlations of rat dorsal CA1 place cells have the topological signature of points sampled uniformly from a three-dimensional hyperbolic ball, not of a low-dimensional Euclidean cube, and the ball's radius grows with the logarithm of exploration time. Place-field sizes are near exponential, and in a Poisson model exponential sizes carry more positional Fisher information than uniform or log-normal ones, with an optimal radius that matches the measured one for the number of CA1 neurons. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-668](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-668.md)); worth reading as, on its own account, the first evidence that neural responses, not stimuli, carry a hyperbolic geometry. Pairwise spike-train correlations of a few dozen active dorsal CA1 cells per session (34 to 56 in the sessions shown), in rats on a novel 48-m track, a 2.5-m track and a 1.8-m box, give Betti curves (clique topology, invariant to any monotone transform of the correlations) that match points sampled uniformly from a 3D hyperbolic ball and fail to match uniform samples from Euclidean cubes of low dimension or shuffled spikes. The fitted radius (10.5–15.5 in units of inverse curvature) grows with the logarithm of exploration time, on scales from seconds to days, as the maximal information acquirable does. Place-field sizes are close to exponential, as the model requires, and in simulation exponentially distributed field sizes give more Fisher information than uniform or log-normal ones, with an optimal radius growing as log N that extrapolates to the radius measured. The "hierarchy" is one of nested place-field sizes; no tree is recovered from the data, and the only null geometry tested is Euclidean with uniform sampling. |
| [LIT-879](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-879.md) v2 | Hyperbolic Neural Networks | Ganea, Bécigneul and Hofmann (NeurIPS 2018), [ARXIV-1805.09112](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.09112). Builds neural-network layers in the Poincaré ball from Möbius gyrovector operations: closed-form exponential and logarithmic maps, parallel transport from the origin as a scaling, geodesic hyperplanes with a closed-form point-to-hyperplane distance, and from them hyperbolic logistic regression, feed-forward layers and GRUs, all reducing to the Euclidean ones as the curvature goes to zero. Linear maps and nonlinearities are lifted through the origin's tangent space, so the curvature acts only through biases and the output distances. Gains over Euclidean models are clear only on a synthetic tree-like task and on separating WordNet subtrees in low dimensions. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-686](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-686.md)); worth reading as the paper that gives the Poincaré ball the operations a neural network is built from, and so shows exactly where hyperbolic geometry enters such a network and where it does not. From Ungar's gyrovector formalism (Möbius addition and scalar multiplication) it derives the exponential and logarithmic maps at any point, parallel transport from the origin as the scaling λ₀/λ_x (Theorem 4), geodesic hyperplanes as exp_p of a tangent orthogonal complement, and the closed-form distance to one (Theorem 5); all of these check out numerically. A linear map or pointwise nonlinearity is lifted as exp₀ ∘ f ∘ log₀, so a stack of such layers is one Euclidean network in log₀ coordinates; the curvature acts only through the bias translations between layers and the distance-based softmax. The evidence is small: 5-dimensional sentence encoders on SNLI, where hyperbolic models are on par or worse, and on a synthetic noisy-prefix task, where they win most when the noise is lowest, each cell the best of three runs; and hyperbolic logistic regression separating WordNet subtrees in pre-trained Poincaré embeddings better than Euclidean hyperplanes do, mostly in 2 to 5 dimensions. |
| [LIT-890](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-890.md) | The power of deeper networks for expressing natural functions | Rolnick and Tegmark (2017; ICLR 2018). Extends [LIT-887](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-887.md)'s 2^n result: one hidden layer of smooth, bias-free units needs exactly ∏(rᵢ+1) neurons to Taylor-approximate x₁^r₁⋯xₙ^rₙ, a deep network O(Σ log rᵢ); sparse polynomials inherit the gap up to a factor 1/c; at depth k a product of n inputs costs at most about 2^(n^(1/k)), conjectured tight. The uniform-approximation lower bounds rest on an unproved step, and the gap grows with degree, not with the number of inputs. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-693](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-693.md)); worth reading as the sequel that turns [LIT-887](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-887.md)'s one depth-separation theorem into a family, and for where the family stops. Proved, for networks without biases and smooth activations with nonzero Taylor coefficients: one hidden layer needs exactly ∏(rᵢ+1) neurons to Taylor-approximate the monomial x₁^r₁⋯xₙ^rₙ, against Σ(7⌈log₂ rᵢ⌉+4) for a deep network; a sparse polynomial with c monomials costs at least 1/c of its dearest monomial; xᵈ costs d+1 shallow against 7⌈log₂ d⌉ deep; and a product of n inputs costs O(n^((k−1)/k)·2^(n^(1/k))) at depth k. The move to uniform approximation, its headline over [LIT-887](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-887.md), rests for the lower bounds on a step the proof asserts and that is false in general (a network can be uniformly within ε of a polynomial while its Taylor coefficients diverge), so only the Taylor-sense lower bounds are established. That depth k needs 2^Θ(n^(1/k)) neurons is a conjecture, backed by one trained-network figure at n = 20 with tanh, outside the theorems' hypotheses. The gap is exponential in a monomial's degree, not in the number of inputs: polynomials of bounded degree, such as the low-order Hamiltonians [LIT-887](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-887.md) calls natural, show none. |

With a third option (reading or writing through without fetching) the lower bound rises to 3, and the algorithm given is 3-competitive ignoring writebacks, 4 counting them; with associative caches the bound becomes the paging ratio. The paper never names rent-or-buy or ski rental; its rent is upkeep paid on an idle copy, and its purchase is the refetch after dropping, the reverse orientation of building a bin. So efficient decentralized search depends on how the long-range links are distributed relative to the lattice, not on the links' existence or on the graph's diameter. Worth reading as the source of the result that a network can have short paths that no searcher using local information can find: on an n × n lattice with long-range links drawn with probability proportional to d^(−r), greedy routing delivers in O((log n)²) expected steps at r = 2 (proved for one local and one long-range contact per node), every decentralized algorithm needs Ω(n^((2−r)/3)) steps for 0 ≤ r < 2 and Ω(n^((r−2)/(r−1))) for r > 2, and r = k in k dimensions is stated without proof. For [CLAIM-310](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-310.md) it shows that findability, with nodes, lattice and link count fixed, turns on how the links are arranged relative to a distance every node can compute, which supports the claim's "as arrangements" half; it narrows "only one distribution" to this family of inverse power laws and to polylogarithmic delivery, and it prices no cost of building the arrangement, so it adds nothing to [QUESTION-114](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-114.md)'s organizing cost. |
| [LIT-1106](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1106.md) | Approximate Nearest Neighbors: Towards Removing the Curse of Dimensionality | Indyk and Motwani (1998), STOC 1998. Approximate nearest-neighbour search in d dimensions reduces, with small overhead, to a decision problem (is there a point within r, or none within (1+ε)r), and that decision problem is solved by locality-sensitive hashing: if hash functions make near pairs collide with probability at least p1 and far pairs with at most p2, then n^ρ random hash tables with ρ = ln(1/p1)/ln(1/p2) answer queries with O(n^ρ) hash evaluations in O(dn + n^{1+ρ}) space, with constant success probability. For Hamming space by bit sampling, and for ℓ_p with p in [1, 2] by embedding, ρ ≤ 1/(1+ε) in the 1999 text (1/ε, for ε > 1, in STOC). The paper also gives the other end of the trade: Õ(d) query time for n·O(1/ε)^d or (nd)^{O(1)} preprocessing. It is an upper bound only: it proves no lower bound, does not claim its exponents are best, solves only the approximate problem with constant probability, and counts preprocessing as space. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the authors' expanded "preliminary version" of December 30, 1999, served from Indyk's MIT directory (people.csail.mit.edu/indyk/nndraft.ps), with its statements compared against the STOC 1998 printed text (pp. 604–613) as posted on a Princeton course page (cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spr04/cos598B/bib/IndykM-curse.pdf); the ACM copy refused requests and Unpaywall and OpenAlex list no open copy. The 2012 Theory of Computing journal version (with Har-Peled) was not read. Worth reading as the origin of locality-sensitive hashing and of the reduction from approximate nearest neighbour to its decision version: hash functions that make near pairs collide more often than far ones give n^ρ tables, O(dn + n^{1+ρ}) space and O(n^ρ) hash evaluations per query, ρ = ln(1/p1)/ln(1/p2), which for Hamming bit sampling is at most 1/(1+ε) in the 1999 text (1/ε, for ε > 1, in STOC), with constant success probability; bucketing gives Õ(d) queries for n·O(1/ε)^d preprocessing. Upper bounds only, approximate only, and preprocessing is counted as space. For [QUESTION-114](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-114.md) it is the first price list for organizing a collection for similarity queries, space paid once against hash evaluations per query, with no amortization over queries and no workload; for [CLAIM-310](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-310.md) it shows the single-arrangement constraint escaped by keeping many random partitions and storing every point in each, paid for in space; it neither extends nor narrows [THEORY-340](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-340.md) and has no bearing on [THEORY-345](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-345.md) or [CLAIM-309](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-309.md). |
| [LIT-1110](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1110.md) | Provenance Semirings | Green et al. (2007), PODS 2007. Annotating each input tuple with an element of a commutative semiring, and computing union and projection with + and join with ·, gives one positive relational algebra (RA+) that is set semantics over the Booleans, bag semantics over the naturals, c-tables over positive Boolean expressions, event tables over sets of outcomes, and lineage over sets of tuple ids. The polynomials N[X] in the tuple ids are the most general such annotation: for any RA+ query and any commutative semiring K, the K-annotated answer is the provenance polynomial evaluated at the input's K-annotations (Theorem 4.3). For datalog the paper needs ω-continuous semirings and formal power series N∞⟦X⟧, with the analogous factorization (Theorem 6.4) and a criterion for infinite coefficients (Theorem 6.5). Everything is positive: no negation, difference or aggregation, and revaluing inputs can only remove output tuples, never add them; trust and deletion propagation are not treated. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 ([NOTE-913](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-913.md)) from the authors' postprint in the University of Pennsylvania's ScholarlyCommons repository (repository.upenn.edu/handle/20.500.14332/8764, file pods07.pdf, 10 pp., posted by permission of ACM), found through Unpaywall and OpenAlex (green, submittedVersion) and fetched through the repository's API because the landing page is script-only. Worth reading as the source of semiring provenance: for positive relational algebra over any commutative semiring the annotated answer is the provenance polynomial in N[X] evaluated at the input annotations, and for datalog over ω-continuous semirings the same holds with formal power series in N∞⟦X⟧ ([THEORY-373](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-373.md), [THEORY-380](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-380.md)). For [QUESTION-105](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-105.md) it shows that retaining one polynomial per output suffices for every revision that re-annotates input facts in a commutative semiring, deletion included, without rerunning the query; it proves no minimality, and it excludes added facts, negation and contraction. Its "why-provenance" is one set of contributing tuples per output, coarser than the witness basis of [LIT-1104](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1104.md) that it cites as the same notion, and its structure for it fails its own semiring axioms. Deletion propagation and trust are not in the paper; deletion follows from Theorem 4.3 as the record's application. For [CLAIM-293](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-293.md) the polynomial separates joint from alternative support but, like topology, leaves the strengths to the valuation; for [CLAIM-306](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-306.md) it has no account of absence. |
| [LIT-1120](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1120.md) | Optimal Hashing-based Time-Space Trade-offs for Approximate Near Neighbors | Andoni et al. (2017), SODA 2017. For c-approximate near-neighbour search (find a point within cr when one lies within r) over n points in Euclidean space, the paper gives a data structure for every pair of exponents with c²√ρq + (c²−1)√ρu ≥ √(2c²−1), using space n^{1+ρu+o(1)} + O(dn) and query time n^{ρq+o(1)} + dn^{o(1)}, on worst-case data (for Hamming and ℓ_1, c√ρq + (c−1)√ρu ≥ √(2c−1)). It proves the curve cannot be beaten by list-of-points structures, the model of all known data-independent hashing schemes, on random instances, and unconditionally in the cell-probe model only at one end (query n^{o(1)}) for one or two probes. So the exact trade between space spent organizing and per-query time is known within the hashing model; outside that model, for more than two probes, it is not, and data-dependent schemes are covered only by conjecture. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the authors' arXiv full version (arXiv:1608.03580v2, 21 May 2017, 62 pp.), which merges the two preprints behind the SODA 2017 extended abstract; the SODA text itself was not seen, and the quantum-information steps of the two-probe proof were followed, not checked. Worth reading as the exact time–space curve for approximate near-neighbour search: for every c > 1, space n^{1+ρu+o(1)} and query time n^{ρq+o(1)} whenever c²√ρq + (c²−1)√ρu ≥ √(2c²−1) in Euclidean space (c√ρq + (c−1)√ρu ≥ √(2c−1) in Hamming and ℓ_1), on worst-case data, and optimal for list-of-points (hashing-based) structures on random instances, with unconditional cell-probe matches only for one or two probes at the n^{o(1)}-query end (n^{(c/(c−1))²−o(1)} words). For [QUESTION-114](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-114.md) it prices organizing against per-query cost exactly within the hashing model, as replication of each point into n^{ρu} lists against n^{ρq} lists scanned, and its closest-pair remark makes the best point depend on the number of queries; it says nothing about workloads, query mixes, build cost beyond space, exact nearest neighbours or structured data, and data-dependent schemes are covered only by conjecture. For [CLAIM-310](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-310.md) it shows overlapping bins are needed for fast similarity queries; for [THEORY-340](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-340.md) it gives the similarity analogue of Yao's lookup floor in the unrestricted cell-probe model at one and two probes; no bearing on [THEORY-345](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-345.md) or [CLAIM-309](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-309.md). |

| [LIT-1151](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1151.md) v2 | Optimal compression of approximate inner products and dimension reduction | Alon & Klartag (2017), FOCS 2017, [ARXIV-1610.00239](https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.00239). For n points of norm at most 1 in R^k and 1/n^0.49 ≤ ε ≤ 0.1, storing every inner product and squared distance to additive ε takes Θ(n log n/ε²) bits once k ≥ log n/ε², Θ(nk log(2 + log n/(ε²k))) for log n ≤ k ≤ log n/ε², and Θ(nk log(1/ε)) below, with an efficient per-point sketch. This gives ae(X) ≤ C log n/log log n for n-point X (improving C log n), ≤ C log λ(X) for doubling X, ≤ C r² for K_r-minor-free graph metrics, e(ℓ₂ᵈ, Z) ≤ C√d, and, with the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma, eₙ(L₂, Z) ≤ C√(log n). | [LIT-1155](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1155.md) v2 | The geometry of graphs and some of its algorithmic applications | Linial, London & Rabinovich (1995), *Combinatorica* 15(2): 215–245. | [LIT-1239](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1239.md) v2 | Localness of energy cascade in hydrodynamic turbulence. I. Smooth coarse graining | Eyink & Aluie (2009). Read it knowing that the theorem is quoted without proof and states no rate in ε and no bound on aggregation error; that the landscape "Simon–Ando condition" is an entrywise proxy, met trivially at low mutation rate even on a flat landscape where there is no time-scale separation; that its leading-eigenvector statement fails when block leading eigenvalues coincide, the stochastic case it invokes; and that (6.2b) is wrong for radius κ ≥ 2. | [LIT-1246](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1246.md) v3 | Diffusion maps | Coifman & Lafon (2006). From a symmetric non-negative kernel, a reversible random walk; its t-step diffusion distance equals the Euclidean distance between eigenvectors weighted by λ_l^t, and truncating where \|λ_l\|^t ≤ δ\|λ₁\|^t gives the diffusion map, whose dimension falls as t grows. An α-normalization by a kernel density estimate gives, as the kernel width ε → 0, a generator with invariant density q^{2(1−α)}: the density-weighted graph Laplacian at α = 0, the Fokker–Planck (Langevin) operator at α = 1/2, and the Laplace–Beltrami operator, free of the density, at α = 1. The diffusion distance D_t is exactly the Euclidean distance between eigenvector coordinates weighted by λ_l^t. The number of steps t is a scale, and the kernel width ε is a second one. An α-normalization makes the small-ε limit the graph Laplacian with a density term (α = 0), the Langevin generator whose invariant density is the sampling density (α = 1/2), or the Laplace–Beltrami operator (α = 1). Read it knowing that Proposition 1's "relative accuracy δ" for the truncated map is wrong (the bound is absolute, [THEORY-745](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-745.md)); that Appendix A's ψ_l = φ_l/π should be φ_l/√π; that the α = 1/2 display, the circle formula, the discrete kernel of §5 and Criterion 4's exponent are misprinted or wrong; that the boundary rate and the heat-kernel proof are incomplete ([THEORY-744](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-744.md)); and that no spectral gap is used anywhere. |

For finite alphabets it gives an achievable rate pair with dispersions (Theorem 5), from which a source is strongly successively refinable if every law in a neighbourhood of it is successively refinable at (D₁, D₂) (Corollary 6). It then uses many refinement stages as a complexity device: with L_n stages the encoder searches L_n small codebooks instead of one exponential one, at a rate penalty of order L_n log n / n, shown for binary-Hamming and Gaussian sources. Nothing in it concerns logarithmic loss. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-980](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-980.md)) in full, from arXiv:1506.03407v2; worth reading for successive refinement at second order (source dispersion): a sufficient condition, Corollary 6, that a source refinable at (D₁, D₂) throughout a neighbourhood of its law is also refinable with both dispersion terms, so that discrete sources under Hamming distortion and the Gaussian under squared error lose nothing even at √n precision; and for layered codes, which use a growing number L_n of refinement stages to trade encoding complexity against rate, with every stage on the rate–distortion curve. | [LIT-1248](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1248.md) v3 | Onsager's conjecture on the energy conservation for solutions of Euler's equation | Constantin, E & Titi (1994). Proves the positive half of Onsager's conjecture: a weak solution of the incompressible Euler equations on the periodic box with u ∈ L³(0,T; B^α_{3,∞}) ∩ C([0,T]; L²) and α > 1/3 conserves energy, because the coarse-grained energy flux across scale ε is O(ε^(3α−1)). Hölder regularity above 1/3 is a special case. It says nothing about solutions below 1/3. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-982](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-982.md)) in full, from the authors' manuscript (the `url:`); worth reading for a complete one-page proof that a weak solution of incompressible Euler with L³-averaged increments scaling as \|y\|^α, α > 1/3, conserves energy ([THEORY-749](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-749.md)), and for its mechanism: the energy flux into scales below a mollification scale ε is a commutator of size ε^(3α−1). Read it knowing that it is the positive half of Onsager's conjecture only and shows nothing about rougher fields: that dissipative solutions exist below 1/3 is Isett (2018) and others, and some rough solutions conserve energy anyway; that its "physical interpretation" (ε̄ = 0) passes to Navier–Stokes and to ensemble averages without proof; that the endpoint 1/3 is not covered; and that the manuscript misprints the exponents in the middle line of its final estimate and integrates (2) over R³ for the box D, neither affecting the result. |
| [LIT-1250](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1250.md) v2 | Diffusion maps, spectral clustering and reaction coordinates of dynamical systems | Nadler, Lafon, Coifman & Kevrekidis (2005; ACHA 2006). For data sampled from p = e^{−U}, it expands the α-normalized diffusion-map operators for small kernel width. The normalized graph Laplacian (α = 0) tends to a backward Fokker–Planck generator with potential 2U, equivalently a Schrödinger operator with potential \|∇U\|² − ΔU. The normalization α = 1/2 gives the generator of the Langevin dynamics ẋ = −∇U + √2ẇ itself. α = 1 gives the Laplace–Beltrami operator, free of the density. So for data from a stochastic system in equilibrium, the leading eigenfunctions approximate the system's slowest modes, and the paper proposes them as reaction coordinates. Examples: Ornstein–Uhlenbeck processes, where the first eigenfunctions parametrize the slow variable; a double well, where the first eigenfunction is ±1 on the two wells; three wells; and the iris data. The expansions are formal, and the printed generators are twice what the stated kernel and time step give. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-986](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-986.md)) in full, from arXiv:math/0503445v1; worth reading for the bridge from a diffusion map to the dynamics behind the data. For samples from p = e^{−U}, the ordinary normalized graph Laplacian (α = 0) tends to a backward Fokker–Planck generator with potential 2U, and the anisotropic normalization α = 1/2 to the generator of the Langevin dynamics with potential U itself, whose slow eigenfunctions the paper proposes as reaction coordinates. It also has worked examples: Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (the finite-ε spectrum λ_k = (τ/(τ+ε))^k), a double well whose first eigenfunction is ±1 on the two wells, and a three-well potential with two pathways. Read it knowing that the generators as printed are twice what the paper's own kernel and time step give (its Ornstein–Uhlenbeck lemma and its equation (32) disagree by that factor, which this reading checked); that "converge" means a formal small-ε expansion of the operator, with the large-sample limit cited and no spectral convergence shown; that its sufficient condition for the first eigenfunctions to depend only on the slow variable is printed the wrong way round; that its double-well example is separable, so the slow coordinate is closed by construction; and that from equilibrium samples the eigenfunctions are recovered well while the slow eigenvalue, the inter-well rate, is not. In what sense slow eigenfunctions are closed coarse variables is the record's addition ([THEORY-762](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-762.md)). The published ACHA version was not reached. |

| [LIT-1255](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1255.md) v2 | A proof of Onsager's conjecture | Isett (2016; Annals 2018). For every α < 1/3 it constructs a nonzero weak solution of the 3D incompressible Euler equations on R × T³, with velocity in C^α and pressure in C^{2α} in space and time, that is identically zero outside a finite time interval, so its kinetic energy is not constant. This is the negative half of Onsager's conjecture; the positive half, conservation above 1/3, is Constantin, E and Titi's. The construction iterates a Main Lemma that adds high-frequency corrections built from Mikado flows, after a new "gluing" step that rearranges the error so that it lives on short, separated time intervals and the corrections never interact. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-974](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-974.md)), skimmed, from arXiv:1608.08301v2: the introduction, the statement of the theorem, the Main Lemma and its three sublemmas, the gluing construction and the convex-integration ansatz, and the whole proof of the theorem from the Main Lemma; the long estimates of §§9–10 and 17 and the appendix were not checked. Worth reading for the negative half of Onsager's conjecture: for every α < 1/3 there is a nonzero weak solution of the 3D incompressible Euler equations on the periodic box, Hölder-continuous with exponent α in space and time, that vanishes outside a finite time interval and so does not conserve energy ([THEORY-763](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-763.md)). With Constantin, E and Titi ([LIT-1248](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1248.md)) it fixes 1/3 as the threshold. Read it knowing that its solutions gain energy from zero and lose it again, so they are not dissipative (admissible) solutions, which came later (Buckmaster, De Lellis, Székelyhidi and Vicol 2019); that they are built by convex integration from the zero solution and so also show non-uniqueness, not that turbulent or vanishing-viscosity limits are of this kind; that the endpoint 1/3, two dimensions and finite-energy solutions on R³ are left open; and that the arXiv v2 copy read is a 2024 revision, not compared with the Annals text. |
| [LIT-1256](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1256.md) v3 | Diffusion wavelets | Coifman & Maggioni (2006). A self-adjoint diffusion operator T defines a multiresolution analysis by thresholding its dyadic powers at a precision ε: V_j is spanned by the eigenvectors with λ^t ≥ ε, so the levels are exactly nested spectral bands set by the operator, not by a partition. The contribution is an algorithm that squares T on each compressed orthonormal basis to build localized scaling functions and wavelets for approximations of these spaces, and compressed dyadic powers that apply the Green's function fast. Proofs cover the uncompressed construction; the compressed scheme's error and cost are argued, not proved. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-984](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-984.md)) in full; worth reading for [QUESTION-217](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-217.md) and [QUESTION-218](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-218.md) as the multilevel case of an operator-induced coarse-to-fine hierarchy. The levels V_j are spanned by the eigenvectors of a self-adjoint diffusion T with λ^t ≥ ε at dyadic t. They are exactly nested, the wavelet spaces W_j are spectral bands of about one octave, and a localized orthonormal basis of each level is built without computing eigenvectors. Read it knowing that the levels are spectral bands and not spatial blocks (the dyadic cubes only shape the basis); that nesting needs no spectral decay, which buys only compression; that the compressed algorithm as written thresholds T^{2^{j−1}}, not T^{2^j−1} as §5.4 and Fig. 1 say, and the paper's own Fig. 9 follows the former ([THEORY-758](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-758.md)); that the indexing of V_j is inconsistent between (4.8), §4.6 and Theorem 27; that only the uncompressed route (Theorems 27 and 29) has proofs, while the compressed scheme's error, localization and O(n log² n) cost are argued or observed; and that the non-self-adjoint extension is asserted, not carried out. |
